newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jordan's king returns to West Bank, meets Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's king returns to West Bank, meets Arafat.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein on Tuesday became the first Arab head of state to visit Palestinian-ruled areas, flying his helicopter to the West Bank he controlled until 1967, witnesses said.
The king arrived in Jericho with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, his host, who had visited him in Amman.
Palestinian officials said the monarch was trying to arrange a meeting between the two of them and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The trip was the king's first to the West Bank since he lost the territory to Israel in the Six-Day War 29 years ago. In 1988, in the heat of the Palestinian uprising, King Hussein gave up all claims to the West Bank, home to a million Palestinians.

King Hussein, Israel's closest Arab ally since signing a peace treaty in 1994, has sided with Arafat of late while distancing himself from the right-wing Netanyahu who took office in June vowing to take a tougher line in peace moves.
Jericho, 24 km (14 miles) northeast of Jerusalem, was the first West Bank town handed over by Israel to Arafat's Palestinian Authority in 1994 under peace deals with the Jewish state.
"It is a very significant visit by the first Arab leader to Palestinian-liberated territories," Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
"It has political significance because it shows support for the Palestinian position and it deepens Palestinian sovereignty in liberated Palestinian areas," he said.

Arafat, wearing his trademark black-and-white keffiyeh, joined the king in saluting a Palestinian honour guard while a Gaza Strip band played the national anthems of both Jordan and the Palestinians. Hundreds applauded.
On the podium a Jordanian flag waved in the wind while the Palestinian flag appeared stuck to the post.
The two leaders, after shaking hands with Palestinian officials, went into a meeting at Arafat's headquarters.
Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh earlier denied news reports Netanyahu was invited to join the meeting, the latest in a flurry of Middle East diplomatic activity.
Israel and the Palestinians have been struggling to reach agreement on their next peace move: Israel's long-promised pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron.
Netanyahu wants changes in the Hebron deal to safeguard 400 Jews living in heavily-armed compounds amidst 100,000 Palestinians in Hebron.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross said that formal talks planned for the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba would be put off at least another day while Israeli-PLO talks continued in Jerusalem.
He said in a statement the present, informal discussions had proven to be productive.
Arafat's spokesman said: "American efforts should continue for several more days in order to narrow the gap, especially since differences in the Israeli and Palestinian positions are still great."

Palestinians opposed demands by Netanyahu to change the Hebron deal signed by the previous Israeli government, Abu Rdainah said. But he said they would be willing to ask U.S. troops to protect settlers -- an idea Netanyahu was likely to reject.
Naveh said the sides had made progress though certain issues might be put to a joint decision by Netanyahu and Arafat.

"If as part of the negotiating process, the need will arise for a meeting between the prime minister and Yasser Arafat, such a meeting will take place but I cannot at the moment read you the exact timetable for such a meeting," he told Israel Radio.
Naveh denied Washington was pressuring Israel to complete a deal before U.S. elections on November 5.
